sourceObservations.observations: Title page explicitly names Lecture Number 21, Linear Control of Manipulators, with institutional branding and a building photograph. No substantive problem premise is present.
Learning-objective page says understand the basics of linear control systems. The outlined lower-right rectangle is empty; this is an orientation page rather than an independent technical claim.
Outline lists introduction, feedback/closed loop, second-order systems and their control, partitioning, trajectory following and disturbance rejection. No new equation or worked example is given.

Two text blocks distinguish linear differential-equation models from the generally nonlinear dynamics of manipulators. Linear control theory is applied through reasonable approximations, not because every robot is globally linear.

The open-loop figure has three desired trajectory signals (position, velocity, acceleration) entering the controller and a torque arrow going to the robot, with no feedback arrow. The displayed inverse-dynamics expression evaluates M, V and G on desired motion. Perfect-model/no-disturbance conditions and correct initial state are needed for exact following; the stepper example is not a claim that every stepper system must be open-loop.

The lower diagram visibly returns actual joint position and velocity from the robot to the controller. All motion/effort signal vectors are labelled N by 1, with N joints. The displayed desired-only inverse-dynamics formula above it contains no servo-error term, so that expression alone is feedforward even though the diagram includes feedback. Position sensors are usual and direct velocity sensing is described as optional.

The equations explicitly define E = desired joint position minus actual position and its derivative with the same sign. The prose associates well-designed feedback with small errors, but a feedback connection alone is not a stability proof and bounded error need not decay to zero under forcing.

The page identifies manipulator control as MIMO and labels independent joint control an approximate treatment as N separate SISO systems. The robot photograph does not imply that actual cross-joint dynamics vanish.

The coordinate arrow points right. In the free-body picture, the spring kx and damper b times velocity arrows point left for positive displacement and velocity. The equation is m times acceleration + b times velocity + kx = 0. Despite the label friction, the force proportional to velocity is linear viscous damping rather than Coulomb friction. Qualitative sluggish/oscillatory claims require positive passive parameters and relative parameter sizes.

The printed characteristic equation is m s squared + b s + k = 0, with roots (-b plus/minus sqrt(b squared - 4mk))/(2m). Pole location determines modal behavior, and the physical passive-system interpretation needs m positive and appropriate b/k signs.

The three cases are positive, negative and zero discriminant, labelled over-, under- and critically damped for the usual passive system. Fastest non-oscillatory is a qualified comparison at fixed natural frequency and suitable response criteria, not a universal promise across arbitrary gains or initial velocities. The simulator hyperlink is supplementary, not a source instruction to navigate.

The real-pole diagram places s1 farther left than s2 on the negative real axis. The accompanying sketch decays toward zero. The two exponential coefficients depend on initial position and velocity. Neglecting the faster mode is a late-time approximation for stable poles with nonzero relevant modal coefficients; an unexcited slow mode cannot dominate.

The derivation correctly expands the conjugate exponential modes with Euler identities, giving cosine coefficient C1 = c1+c2 and sine coefficient C2 = i(c1-c2). These are real for a real motion with conjugate complex modal coefficients. The uppercase C constants on this page must not be confused with the earlier lowercase complex coefficients.

The actual formula is x = r exp(lambda t) cos(mu t - delta), with r from the real cosine/sine coefficients and atan2(sine coefficient, cosine coefficient). This page switches back to lowercase c notation, creating an ambiguity with the preceding complex coefficients. The pole pair is shown in the left half plane and the graph oscillates with a decaying envelope, requiring negative lambda.

The normalized polynomial has coefficients 2 zeta omega_n and omega_n squared. Visible square roots are present in omega_n = sqrt(k/m), zeta = b/(2 sqrt(km)), and mu = omega_n sqrt(1-zeta squared). Text extraction loses some radicals; the image resolves them. Positive m and k are needed, and real damped frequency uses the underdamped range.

The repeated-pole solution visibly includes the t multiplier: (c1+c2 t) exp[-b t/(2m)]. The pole diagram has a repeated negative real root and the response sketch decays without sinusoidal cycling. The limit with exp(-a t) needs a>0. The fastest-response caption remains a qualified comparison, not a universal initial-state guarantee.

An applied force f arrow points right, matching positive x, on the mass-spring-damper diagram. The forced equation is m x-double-dot + b x-dot + kx = f. Sensors and an actuator are introduced to reshape the natural response, not to remove physical mass or stiffness.

The diagram returns actual x through the position gain and actual velocity through the velocity gain; both branches enter the summing junction with minus signs. Substitution gives effective damping b+kv and stiffness k+kp. These direct force-feedback gains have N/m and N s/m units and must not be confused with later normalized servo gains.

The critical condition is b_prime = 2 sqrt(m k_prime). With m = b = k = 1 and desired k_prime = 16, the direct force gains are Kp = 15 and Kv = 7. Negative individual gains can still leave positive effective damping and stiffness; strict asymptotic stability requires both effective coefficients positive for m > 0.
Model-based compensation and servo feedback are separate portions. Compensation makes the controlled equation simpler under an exact model; it does not physically remove the spring, damper, or mass.

The printed decomposition is f = alpha f_prime + beta, with alpha = m and beta = b xdot + k x using actual state. Exact cancellation gives xddot = f_prime. The normalized command has acceleration units; beta is force. Model mismatch prevents exact cancellation.

The normalized servo command is f_prime = -kv xdot -kp x, giving xddot + kv xdot + kp x = 0. The visible critical-damping radical is kv = 2 sqrt(kp). Normalized kp and kv have units s^-2 and s^-1, unlike the direct force gains.

The block diagram multiplies the normalized servo command by m and adds positive b xdot + k x compensation before the physical plant. The example uses m = b = k = 1, normalized kp = 16 and kv = 8. Expanding the physical force gives -15 x -7 xdot, matching the direct-force example.

Desired position and its first two derivatives are available. With e = xd -x, the tracking command is f_prime = xddot_d + kv edot + kp e. Coefficient shaping is an ideal model result; the general claim about obtaining any desired response needs actuator, sensing, and modeling qualifications.

The actual diagram forms e = xd - x and edot = xdot_d - xdot, feeds both positively into the normalized command with desired acceleration, multiplies by m, and adds actual-state compensation. Combining with the exact unit-mass model gives eddot + kv edot + kp e = 0. Any-response wording is an ideal coefficient-design statement, not an actuator-unlimited guarantee.

The disturbance arrow enters the physical force summing node after the m block with a minus sign. The printed equation uses a positive f_dist on the error side without writing division by mass. If the arrow is a physical resisting force F_dist, the normalized right side is F_dist/m. If an external force instead assists positive motion, its error-equation sign is negative.

The displayed bound is max_t f_dist(t) < a, with no absolute-value bars. A two-sided magnitude bound and a stable disturbance-to-error system are needed for the stated bounded-output conclusion. Bounded error need not converge to zero. The statement that disturbances do not make the system unstable is conditional on the stable model and bounded input.

The steady-state calculation sets derivatives to zero and gives e_ss = f_dist/kp. Raising a positive kp reduces the magnitude for fixed disturbance while stability and feasibility are maintained. Never zero needs a nonzero constant disturbance and finite nonzero kp; zero disturbance permits zero error.

The integral command adds ki times the integral of error. On the actual pixels the differentiated right side has a visible dot over f_dist, unlike extraction that can lose it. The differentiated equation is third order and the constant-disturbance steady conclusion requires stability, nonzero ki, and compatible integral state. Positive gains alone do not guarantee third-order stability. Differentiation does not erase the original integral equation initial-condition constraint.

Summary repeats the linear approximation, feedback/MIMO-to-SISO simplification, three damping cases, model/servo partition, trajectory tracking and disturbance/integral control. No new independent equation or example; the stability qualifications from earlier pages still apply.
Reference-only page cites J. J. Craig, Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control, third edition, Pearson Prentice Hall, 2005. No new technical assessment target.
Thank-you ending page, with no new technical content.

independentAnswers.reasoning: A justified operating-regime approximation yields a linear model; vector notation and sensors do not remove physical nonlinearities.
The displayed inverse-dynamics controller takes desired position, velocity and acceleration, not measured tracking errors.
The open-loop drawing has no actual-output feedback path, so it cannot directly correct measured tracking error.
Multiplication gives M[1,-2]^T = [0,-5]^T. Adding [1,0]^T and [3,4]^T gives [4,-1]^T N m.
Exact inverse-dynamics tracking needs the exact model, matching initial position and velocity, and no unmodeled forcing; otherwise equal commanded acceleration is not enough.
The two returning signals in the diagram are actual position and velocity.
For N joints, each joint-variable signal is an N by 1 vector. This does not imply independent mechanical dynamics.
The printed desired-state equation is feedforward; the actual-state feedback drawing alone does not insert an unwritten error term into that equation.
Desired minus actual gives E = 0.8 - 0.5 = 0.3 rad and Edot = -0.2 - 0.1 = -0.3 rad/s.
Feedback can reduce errors under suitable design; neither feedback presence nor bounded error alone guarantees stability or zero error.
The approximation uses N separate SISO design problems in place of the coupled MIMO dynamics, without claiming physical coupling disappears.
With positive rightward displacement and velocity, spring and viscous damper forces both point left: -kx and -b xdot.
The acceleration is (-8(0.5)-3(-1))/2 = -0.5 m/s^2.
A force proportional to signed velocity is viscous damping, unlike a fixed-magnitude sign-dependent Coulomb law.
For x = exp(st), xdot = sx and xddot = s^2 x, so division by the nonzero exponential gives ms^2 + bs + k = 0.
For positive mass and stiffness, a negative b^2-4mk discriminant gives a complex-conjugate underdamped pair.
For m = k = 1, b = 1 has negative discriminant, b = 2 zero, and b = 3 positive: underdamped, critical, overdamped.
The familiar fastest nonoscillatory comparison needs a fixed natural-frequency or otherwise controlled comparison; critical damping is not universally fastest across all gains and initial states.
A second-order homogeneous response has two integration constants fixed by initial displacement and velocity.
x = 3 exp(-2t) - 2 exp(-3t) gives x(0)=1 and xdot(0)=-6+6=0.
The stable pole closer to zero decays more slowly and dominates sufficiently late only if its mode coefficient is nonzero.
If the slow-mode coefficient is exactly zero, the slow pole is not excited in that natural response; another excited mode determines decay.
Combining conjugate modes gives exp(lambda t)[A cos(mu t)+B sin(mu t)], with real A and B for a real physical response.
Euler expansion yields cosine coefficient c1+c2 and sine coefficient i(c1-c2). For a real response the complex coefficients are conjugates.
For real A=-3 and B=4, r=sqrt(9+16)=5 and delta=atan2(4,-3) lies in quadrant II, since r cos(delta)=A and r sin(delta)=B.
With nonzero amplitude, lambda < 0 gives an exponentially decaying oscillatory envelope; phase does not determine stability.
omega_n=sqrt(16/4)=2 rad/s and zeta=8/(2 sqrt(4*16))=0.5.
lambda=-zeta omega_n=-1 s^-1 and mu=omega_n sqrt(1-zeta^2)=sqrt(3) rad/s.
Zero damping ratio at positive natural frequency yields a pure imaginary pole pair and sustained oscillation for a nonzero excited mode, not exponential decay.
At a repeated root, two copies of exp(st) are dependent, while t exp(st) supplies the second independent solution.
x=(1+4t)exp(-4t) satisfies x(0)=1 and xdot(0)=4-4=0.
For arbitrary finite constants, polynomial times exp(-at) tends to zero when a>0; a=0 or a<0 does not ensure decay.
Substituting f=-Kv xdot-Kp x into m xddot+b xdot+kx=f gives effective damping b+Kv and stiffness k+Kp.
Both measured position and velocity enter the direct force sum negatively, producing restoring and damping contributions.
Desired k_prime=16 gives Kp=16-1=15 N/m; critical b_prime=2 sqrt(1*16)=8 gives Kv=8-1=7 N s/m.
The negative individual gains still leave effective damping and stiffness equal to 4, so the characteristic polynomial is (s+2)^2 and the origin is asymptotically stable.
For positive mass, strict asymptotic stability of the second-order effective polynomial requires positive effective damping and stiffness; zero coefficients introduce boundary cases.
Model compensation cancels known physical terms in the ideal equation, while the servo portion then shapes the simpler residual response.
Setting alpha=m and beta=b xdot+kx yields m xddot = m f_prime after exact cancellation.
Since xddot=f_prime, the normalized command is acceleration, measured in m/s^2, not force.
Substitution with estimated parameters gives m xddot=mhat f_prime+(bhat-b)xdot+(khat-k)x, retaining mismatch terms.
For unit-mass normalized critical damping, kv=2 sqrt(kp)=2 sqrt(25)=10 s^-1.
Direct force Kp has units N/m, whereas normalized acceleration kp has units s^-2; they are not numerically interchangeable without mass scaling and compensation.
The model-based branch adds positive actual-state b xdot+kx to cancel the plant's negative spring/damper contributions.
The printed example has alpha=1 kg, beta=(1 N s/m)xdot+(1 N/m)x, and normalized critical kv=8 s^-1 when kp=16 s^-2.
The normalized servo plus compensation is -16x-8xdot+x+xdot=-15x-7xdot in the example's physical units, identical to the earlier direct force gains.
The trajectory command uses desired position and its first two time derivatives.
With e=xd-x, positive kp e and kv edot correct the tracking error, while desired acceleration supplies feedforward.
Subtracting xddot=xddot_d+kv edot+kp e from desired acceleration yields eddot+kv edot+kp e=0.
Without desired-acceleration feedforward, subtraction leaves eddot+kv edot+kp e=xddot_d, so a moving desired trajectory forces the error dynamics.
The diagram first forms the normalized feedforward-plus-error command, then multiplies by mass and adds physical model compensation.
Ideal coefficient selection shapes the mathematical response but cannot override physical actuator limits, imperfect sensing or model error.
A resisting physical force subtracted after the mass block gives actual acceleration f_prime-F_dist/m and hence positive F_dist/m on the error-equation right side.
An assisting external force added at the plant gives actual acceleration f_prime+F_ext/m and hence negative F_ext/m in the desired-minus-actual error equation.
Disturbance rejection aims to preserve useful performance and limit errors, not to guarantee removal of every external influence.
A magnitude bound |d(t)| <= a for all relevant times is two-sided; a one-sided upper bound permits unbounded negative disturbances.
A bounded input yields bounded error only for a stable disturbance-to-error map with appropriate finite initial state; bounded forcing alone is insufficient.
A stable error response may approach a nonzero constant d/kp; bounded does not mean zero.
At a constant-disturbance equilibrium, eddot=edot=0, so kp e_ss=d and e_ss=d/kp.
A 6 N resisting force on 2 kg gives d=3 m/s^2. With kp=3 s^-2, e_ss=1 m.
For the same constant disturbance, doubling positive kp halves the equilibrium error if the loop remains stable and the model applies.
The never-zero claim is valid only for a nonzero constant disturbance and finite nonzero proportional gain; zero disturbance permits zero error.
The integral controller uses ki z with zdot=e and z(t)=z(0)+integral_0^t e(tau) d tau, preserving stored integral state.
Integral state has units m s, so ki must have units s^-3 to make ki z an acceleration.
Differentiating eddot+kv edot+kp e+ki z=d with zdot=e gives e''' +kv eddot+kp edot+ki e=dot(d). The source pixels show the disturbance derivative.
For a stable settled integral loop and nonzero ki, constant disturbance has dot(d)=0 and the differentiated equilibrium gives e_ss=0; stability is essential.
At zero steady error, the stored integral term supplies the disturbance balance: z_ss=d/ki=4/2=2 m s.
s^3+2s^2+s+12 factors as (s+3)(s^2-s+4); the quadratic roots have real part +1/2, proving positive gains alone need not stabilize the PID loop.

Differentiation removes the constant forcing from the differential equation but not the original integral-state compatibility condition. The initial z must still satisfy the undifferentiated equation.
